name: ring-virtual-nodes
description: the ring with virtual nodes s0_0, s0_1, s1_0 and key k0 moving clockwise
see: a circle with several labelled points such as s0_0 and s1_1 and a key k0 with an arrow clockwise to the next node
material:
[p.80] Non-Uniform Key Distribution It's possible for key distribution on the ring to be uneven. For example, if servers are placed as shown in Figure 5-11, most keys end up on server 2. Meanwhile, server 1 and server 3 don't store any data. Virtual Nodes To fix issues with uneven distribution, we use a technique called virtual nodes or replicas. A virtual node represents a real server. Each server has several virtual nodes on the ring. In Figure 5-12, both server 0 and server 1 have 3 virtual nodes each. The number 3 refers to how many virtual nodes each server has.

[p.81] Understanding Virtual Nodes in Distributed Systems In real-world systems, we often use more virtual nodes than just a few. Instead of just using a label like s0 for server 0, we use s0_0, s0_1, and s0_2. These represent server 0 on the ring. Similarly, s1_0, s1_1, and s1_2 represent server 1. With these virtual nodes, each server handles multiple partitions. Partitions are sections of data. For example, partitions marked with s0 are managed by server 0, while those marked with s1 are managed by server 1. To find out which server holds a particular key, we start at the key's location and move clockwise around the ring. We look for the first virtual node we see. For example, in Figure 5-13, to find out where the key k0 is stored, we go clockwise from k0's location. We encounter the virtual node s1_1, which points to server 1.

[p.82] Virtual Nodes and Key Distribution As the number of virtual nodes increases, the keys are spread out more evenly. This happens because the standard deviation gets smaller with more virtual nodes. Standard deviation shows how much data varies or spreads out. Research from an online study shows that with one or two hundred virtual nodes, the standard deviation falls between 5% (for 200 virtual nodes) and 10% (for 100 virtual nodes) of the average. When we add more virtual nodes, the standard deviation becomes smaller. However, we need more storage space to keep data about virtual nodes. This is a tradeoff. We can adjust the number of virtual nodes to meet our system's needs. Finding Affected Keys When a server is added or removed, some data must be moved around. How can we find out which keys need to be moved? In Figure 5-14, when server 4 is added to the ring, we start checking from s4 (the new node). We go anticlockwise around the ring until we reach a server (s3). The keys between s3 and s4 are the ones that need to be moved to s4.
